To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) at wide angles, the response of a calorimeter to hadron jets is significantly different from the response to electrons; (2) the response of the calorimeter depends on the energy sharing of the jet between the electromagnetic and hadron calorimeters; (3) the response of a hadron calorimeters to hadron jets depends on the type and momentum of the jet fragments; and (4) the calorimeter resolution is not Gaussian for low momentum particles.

1) the energy resolution of a calorimeter for low momentum hadron showers is significantly worse than for high momentum ones, and 2) a hadron calorometer can be made to have a response to pions which is close to that of an electromagnetic calorimeter, but at the cost of a significant degradation of its resolution for low momentum hadrons.
The response of hadron calorimeters to low momentum particles is not linear, and the deviation from linearity increases as the momentum decreases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects which are important in the hadronic environment of a storage ring.

the response to hadrons of a calorimeter with an iron absorber and scintillator active material, and the effects of the calorimeter on the angular distribution of hadrons in the final state of a reaction.
the problems of hadron calorimeter response in a wide angle environment, and the effects of different hadron calorimeter characteristics on the calorimeter response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the calorimeter response to low momentum hadrons is a complex function of the energy sharing between calorimeters, of the calorimeter type, and of the incident particle.

the hadron calorimeter response is a complicated function of the energy sharing between different calorimeters, of the energy sharing within a given calorimeter, of the angle of the incident particle, and of the particle type.
there is no simple and general answer to the question: "How do I build an optimal hadron calorimeter?"
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a calorimeter which has a fine grain structure is not necessarily superior to a coarser structure, but that the best results are achieved by combining the two. 12 refs., 7 figs.
, for a storage ring calorimeter, the response to hadrons is not a simple function of incident particle type or momentum.
a hadron calorimetry program is needed to complement the existing electromagnetic calorimetry program. 10 refs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a 4π hadron calorimeter with good resolution at wide angles will require a very large number of fine grain lead absorbers.
hadron calorimeters should not be assumed to have the same response to all particles, even when the calorimeter is constructed of the same material and with the same granularity.
the response to very low momentum particles is very different in a lead calorimeter than in an iron calorimeter.
